sentences.html: A STRANGER'S FAVORITE SONG
Roya Publication No. 13
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS
Ali cannot answer the three questions everyone asks at his father’s memorial: what song he loved, what food he loved, what place he loved.
He realises, sitting in the good chair reserved for a son, in a rented hall in Orange County eleven thousand kilometres from the grave, that he has spent a lifetime loving a man he barely knew.

A STRANGER’S FAVORITE SONG moves between a marriage that ended in silence rather than in shouting, a house in Mirdamad that stopped being a retreat and became the only place left, and the long, one-sided last months that followed — months measured out in Friday phone calls, voice messages, a housekeeper’s hand holding up a phone, and a silence that slowly replaced a voice.

Between the grief chapters sit others: a massage parlour on Westwood Boulevard visited out of pure stubborn devotion, a father’s operatic fury over a badly parked car, a joke about grandchildren that turned out, in the end, to have been entirely true.

It is a novella about the particular ache of losing someone twice — once to forgetting, and once to death — and about the strange, late mercy of understanding a father only after you have caught yourself becoming him.
A book of the Chronicle.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book began with a simple, uncomfortable question: how well do we actually know the people we love most, once we strip away the assumption that closeness and knowledge are the same thing?

Many of us could sit at a parent’s memorial and be asked their favourite song, their favourite meal, their favourite place in the world — and come up empty, not for lack of love, but for lack of the specific, unglamorous conversations that never felt urgent until there was no longer any time left to have them.
The book is also an attempt to sit honestly with a harder question: what does grief look like when the person you are mourning had already lost so much of himself before his body finally followed?

And what does it look like when you could not go — when the country he died in is one you are not able to enter, and the whole of the ending reaches you through a telephone held up by somebody else’s hand?
Is it betrayal to feel relief when the waiting ends?
I don’t think so.
I think relief and grief are frequently the same weather system, arriving from different directions at once, and that pretending otherwise only isolates the people going through it.

Alzheimer’s appears here as a kind of speculative fiction within the fiction — an attempt, offered humbly and without any claim to authority, to imagine what time and self might feel like from the inside of a mind that is quietly coming apart.
No one can know this for certain.
I hope the attempt is more useful than the silence would have been.
Finally: I don’t think you can really understand your own parents until you have caught yourself doing the thing they did.
Not the good things.
The other one — the silence across a table from a person you love, the not-saying, the going somewhere in your own head while somebody waits.
That understanding often arrives too late to use on the actual relationship.
This book is, in part, about what to do with it anyway.
Chew Z
CHAPTER ONE
[PRESENT]

I had put on the same dark suit I own for exactly this purpose — weddings on one end of its life, funerals on the other, nothing in between that seemed to require it — and stood in front of the mirror longer than the task warranted, the way you do when you are not actually checking your appearance so much as delaying the moment you have to walk out the door and become the son everyone is about to need you to be.
She adjusted my collar without being asked, a small unnecessary correction that felt, that morning, like the only thing anyone had done for me in days that wasn’t a condolence.
The tea had gone cold in front of everyone at once, as if the room had agreed on it without speaking.
I sat where I had been placed — the good chair, the one nearest the photograph, the one reserved for a son — and let the condolences move past me like weather.
God rest him.
He was a good man.
He is at peace now.
The words arrived in the same order from every mouth, in two languages, and I nodded at each of them with the same tilt of the head, and somewhere behind my sternum a small animal was pacing.
I want to be exact about where this was, because the exactness is the whole of it.
It was not Tehran.

It was a rented hall behind a Persian restaurant in Irvine, California, on a Sunday afternoon in February, with too much fluorescent light for the occasion and folding chairs that had clearly been used for weddings as often as funerals, the same stackable chairs pressed into service for whatever life happened to be asking of them that week.
My father had been buried six days earlier, in Tehran, in the morning, next to his mother, and I had watched it on a telephone propped against a cup.
My brother had watched it on the same telephone, from the same sofa, having driven the forty minutes to sit on it.
Neither of us could go.
The reasons are two other books long and a pair of hands long and, in Amir’s case, his own, and I am not going to make this book carry them.
So my aunts did what the women of that family have always done, which is build a room around a thing nobody could bear.
Farah booked the hall.
Shirin ordered the food.
Someone had put out too much of it, which felt correct, which felt like the one detail in the entire afternoon that would have met with his approval.

The photograph on the easel beside my chair was the one my mother had chosen and sent from Tehran — a decent one, taken by some cousin at a wedding years back, my father caught mid-sentence, one hand slightly raised as if making a point about the rice, which, knowing him, he very well might have been.
It was a good photograph.
It did not look like a man who had spent his last months disappearing by degrees.
It looked like someone about to tell you something at length, whether you had asked or not, and I found myself staring at it throughout the afternoon the way you stare at a door you expect to open.
It was my aunt Farah who asked the first question, and she asked it kindly, the way you’d ask a child to recite something he’d surely been taught.
“What was his favourite song, azizam?
We should play it.
For the room.”
I opened my mouth.
Nothing arrived to fill it.
I thought of the car, decades back, my father’s hand on the dial, always moving, never landing.
I thought of the radio left on in every room of every place he ever slept, for company more than for listening.
I could not, if the hall had been on fire and the answer the only water, have named one song my father loved enough to ask for twice.
“I’m not sure,” I said.
“He liked — he had the radio on a lot.
I don’t think he had one song.”
Farah’s face did the thing faces do when they are deciding whether to press.
She let it go.
She patted my knee instead, which was worse.
It was Mr Rostami who asked the second one, an hour later, holding a plate of dates he had not touched.

He was a retired man from three doors down from my aunt’s, who had known my father only in California, only in the years my father spent there, and who had, I gathered, spent a great many afternoons with him in a lawn chair in my aunt’s garden discussing the moral collapse of everything.
“Kamran loved his food.
Everyone knew this.
What was his favourite dish?
My wife will make it, in his memory, next Friday.”

And I, thirty-seven years old, a man who builds rooms for a living in which strangers are told exactly what to feel and in what order, discovered that I did not know my father’s favourite dish either.

I knew that my father ate constantly, joyfully, without apparent discrimination — kebab from the stall, his mother’s stew on the holidays, whatever the delivery boy brought at eleven at night when he couldn’t sleep, a foam container of something from a strip mall in Westwood eaten standing up in a car park with total seriousness.
I knew my father loved the act of eating the way other men love a sport.
I did not know which team.
“He liked everything,” I said, which was true, and which was also a way of saying I don’t know, dressed for company.
The third question I saw coming from across the room, the way you see a wave a half-second before it reaches you, and there was nothing to do but let it reach me.
It was Amir, my own brother, four years older and therefore — in the particular arithmetic of Iranian sons — somehow always more forgiven for not knowing things.
He crouched by my chair and said, low, just for me:
“Was there a place he loved?
For the — you know.
When people ask where to go, to remember him.
A place.”
I looked at my brother’s face, which had our father’s eyebrows and our mother’s mouth, and felt something in my chest do a slow, complete turn, like a key finding the wrong lock.
“I don’t know, Amir,” I said.
“I don’t think he went anywhere.
I think he just — stayed.”
My brother nodded, as if this were an answer, and it was, though not the kind either of us could use for a plaque or a programme or a toast.
It was the truest thing either of us had said all day, and it explained absolutely nothing, and it was going to have to be enough, because it was all we had.
I sat with my cold tea until the room emptied into its cars, and thought: I have his eyebrows.
I have, apparently, his temper, according to the woman who adjusted my collar.
I have fifteen years of Fridays and Saturdays and voice messages that said call when you can in a voice that got thinner every year.
And I could not tell one stranger, in the week we buried him, what song he would have wanted playing while we did it.

Outside, the light was doing the ordinary, indecent thing light does on days like this in Southern California — arriving gold and generous over a car park, over a row of minivans, over nothing that had asked for it.

She found me by the car and didn’t ask what was wrong, which I have come, in the four years we have been doing this, to understand as its own kind of gift — the not-asking, the willingness to simply stand next to a person until whatever is happening in them finishes happening.
“You didn’t have to have an answer,” she said eventually, which was kind, and which also wasn’t true, not in the way that mattered.
I hadn’t needed an answer for Farah, or for Mr Rostami, or even really for Amir.
I had needed the answer for myself, for some private accounting I hadn’t known I was keeping until the questions arrived and found the ledger empty.
I thought, not for the first time and not for the last: what do you do with a grief for a man you loved completely and knew barely at all?
There is no ritual for that particular shape.
You just sit in the good chair, in the wrong country, and let people ask you questions, and discover the size of the silence where the answers should have been.
CHAPTER TWO
[BEFORE]

I wasn’t there for any of this, which means everything in this chapter comes to me secondhand — from three photographs, a handful of my mother’s stories told at the exact same pace every time she told them, and a kind of guessing I’ve allowed myself because a son is entitled to imagine his father young at least once.

Before any of that, before my mother, there was a version of my father I know even less about — a boy from a house in the south of the city whose father repaired sewing machines and whose mother ran a kitchen like a small, fierce general, and who was clever in the specific brutal way that country used to reward.

He got into Sharif, and the universities closed under him for three years, and he married my mother in the middle of that closure, and came out an engineer the year the war ended, already a father twice over and already, for five years, on my grandfather’s payroll, putting lifts into a city that was throwing up towers faster than it could staff them, and somewhere in those years he built himself, the way you build anything — an accent from the north, a collar, a way of standing in a room — so completely that by the time I was old enough to notice, there was no seam in it anywhere.
In the photographs he is thin.
This is the first thing that surprises me every time I look at them, because the man I knew filled a doorway the way a good meal fills a plate — generously, a little over the edge.

But in the photographs he is thin and dark-haired and wearing a shirt with a collar so wide it looks like it is trying to fly off his shoulders, and he is looking at my mother the way men in old photographs are not supposed to look — not posed, not aware of the camera at all, looking at her like she was the only interesting thing that had ever happened in that room.

My mother says they met at her cousin’s engagement party, where he had not been invited and had come anyway, on the arm of a colleague of a colleague, because — and she always laughs here, every single time, forty years of laughing at the same joke — “your father could smell a party with good food in it from two neighbourhoods away.”
He asked her to dance twice.
She said no twice.
The third time he didn’t ask.
He simply appeared next to her with two plates of food he’d assembled from the buffet like he was building something structural, and said, “You haven’t eaten.

A woman who hasn’t eaten cannot be trusted to make good decisions, like refusing to dance with me,” and handed her a plate, and she took it, and that — she says, and I believe her, because it is the single most him thing I have ever heard — was the whole courtship, more or less.
He fed her into liking him.
There was a second act to this story that my mother only told me once, late, on a night when she’d had enough wine to let the guard down a little.

He had asked her, three weeks after the engagement party, to marry him — not on one knee, not with a ring he could afford yet, but standing outside her father’s gate in Elahieh at an hour a young man from the south had no business standing outside anyone’s gate in the north, holding a single stem of jasmine he had apparently taken from a neighbour’s wall on the walk over, uninvited and unashamed about it.

“I don’t have anything to offer you yet,” he told her, “except that I will never once let you go hungry, and I think that might be worth more than people give it credit for.” My mother says she laughed at him.
She said yes anyway, before the laugh had even finished, which she describes now as the only decision in her entire life she made faster than she should have and would still make again.
My grandfather’s reaction to the engagement, as best I can reconstruct it, was somewhere between amusement and calculation.

Yousef was a man who had founded a company out of nothing and spent thirty years making it into something that put up half the towers in the north of the city, and he looked at the thin engineer at his gate the way he looked at everything, which was as a problem with a solution in it.
The solution was a job.

My father went to work for my grandfather’s firm within the year, putting lifts into the buildings my grandfather’s firm was putting up, and I have come to understand, much too late, that this was the first gift my father ever accepted from that family and the last thing he ever took from anyone without paying for it twice.

My grandmother came around the way the women in both families apparently always did, by way of the kitchen — but it was my father’s mother, Katayoun, who administered the only exam that family ever actually gave anyone.
She invited my mother to the house in Mirdamad and tested her not on suitability but on appetite, on whether she’d take a second helping without being asked twice.
My mother, who was an art historian and had been raised in a house with a Steinway nobody played, took the second helping.
She still describes it as the most important examination she ever passed.
The wedding itself, by my mother’s account, was small and slightly chaotic in the specific way weddings are when one family has money and the other has a mother who will not be told how to cook.

My mother remembers my father being nearly an hour late to his own ceremony, having stopped, en route, to resolve some dispute at the caterer’s over a shortage of rice that he had personally appointed himself to fix, arriving finally with his collar crooked and an explanation that somehow left everyone laughing instead of angry, which she says was the moment she understood, fully and for the first time, exactly what she’d agreed to marry.
“I married a man who couldn’t walk past a kitchen with a problem in it,” she told me once.
“I just didn’t know yet that it would eventually become the only kind of problem he was willing to walk toward.”
I try to picture it and I can.
That part is easy.
The part I have never been able to picture, no matter how many times my mother tells it, is what he sounded like when he was trying.
I know what he sounded like defeated — thin-voiced, over a phone line, forty years later, saying call when you can like it cost him something.

I know what he sounded like furious — I have that recording permanently, somewhere in the part of the brain that keeps such things, a specific pitch reserved for parking attendants and slow waiters and the men who ran the car park at my aunt Shirin’s condominium in Irvine.
But I have no recording, no memory, no photograph that captures sound, of what he sounded like courting.

I have had to build it myself, out of the shape of the story, and in my private reconstruction he sounds like a much younger, much luckier version of the man who used to laugh so hard at his own jokes — with no sound, shoulders going, that was how he laughed — that he’d have to put his fork down.
For a few years, by every account I have gathered, they were happy in the plain, undocumented way people were happy before everyone carried a camera in their pocket to prove it.
There are no professional photographs of this part.
There is my father, standing outside a rented apartment with a bag of pistachios the size of a pillow, mid-laugh at something my mother said, caught by a neighbour’s borrowed camera.
There is my mother, pregnant with Amir, sitting on a step, squinting into sun, my father’s hand visible at the edge of the frame, resting on her shoulder like he’d forgotten to take it away.
He was, in this period, by every account, a man who liked his life.
He liked the little apartment.
He liked being newly a husband.

He apparently liked, with a passion my mother describes as “genuinely a little insane,” any meal eaten outside the house, on the theory — his own, stated often, according to her — that “food cooked by someone who is paid to care about it tastes like they care about it, and food cooked out of duty tastes like duty.” He would say this to his own mother’s face, at her own table in Mirdamad, and she would swat him with a spoon, and he would eat two more helpings to make up for the insult, and everyone would laugh, and this — this specific triangle of insult, spoon, second helping — apparently happened at nearly every meal for years, and never once stopped being funny to any of them.
There is one more story from this period my mother tells that I’ve never quite known what to do with.

In the second year of the marriage, before either of us existed, my father spent an entire month’s wages — money that should have gone toward the deposit on a better flat — on a used record player he found in a shop window, for no reason my mother could ever get out of him beyond

“a house should have music in it, even if we don’t.” They owned exactly four records between them, borrowed mostly, and my mother says he’d play the same two sides on Friday mornings, cooking eggs badly and singing along even worse, entirely unconcerned with how he sounded, until the neighbour upstairs began banging a broom handle on his floor as a form of protest.
My father took the broom handle, my mother says, as a compliment — proof the music was loud enough to matter to somebody.
I have never been able to find out what was on those four records.

My mother doesn’t remember, or says she doesn’t, and the record player did not survive the move to Elahieh, where there was a Steinway to stand in its place that nobody ever played, and so this is one more entry in the long list of things about my father that exist only as the outline of a story, with the actual content missing.
I did not know this man.
I want to be careful and say that plainly, here, in the middle of writing him as if I did.
The man in these stories — quick, hungry, funny, reckless enough to stand at a rich man’s gate with a stolen flower — is not a man I ever once met.

By the time I was old enough to form memory, he had already started the long, slow business of becoming someone else, and I have spent most of my life assuming that quieter, heavier man was simply who my father was, the way you assume a house has always looked the way it looks the day you’re born into it, never wondering what stood on the lot before.
It turns out a whole different man stood there first.

I only found him after he was already gone, going through the photographs my mother scanned and sent me one at a time over a fortnight because she could not bear to send them all at once, sitting on the floor of an apartment in Los Angeles while the woman I live with slept in the next room, looking at a thin man in a wide collar laughing so hard he’d had to put his fork down, thinking: I would have liked you.
I think I would have liked you very much.
I’m sorry I only got the ending.
CHAPTER THREE
[INTERIOR I]
A note on these sections: no one can know what this was like from the inside.
What follows is speculation — Ali’s, and mine — offered not as fact but as the only kind of understanding available when the person who could confirm or deny it is no longer able to answer.
These chapters grow stranger as the book goes on.
The kitchen smells like his mother’s hands.

He is lying somewhere — a bed, a good bed, a bed with rails on it that he does not need to check for because his hands have found them already — and the smell arrives before anything else does, the way it always has, saffron and browning onion and the particular hot-metal smell of a pot lid lifted too soon, and for a moment this is simply Tuesday, or some Tuesday, one of many, and he is young enough that being called to the table still feels like an event worth having opinions about.
He is aware, distantly, of a voice.
It has been talking for a while.

It has a shape he recognises the way you recognise a song from only its opening note — familiar, warm, belonging to him in some way he can’t currently name — but the words are arriving slightly out of order, or perhaps he is simply choosing, without deciding to, which ones to keep.
Baba.
He keeps that one.

It sits in his chest like a coal, warm, wanted, though whose baba, and in relation to what, has slipped somewhere just behind him, the way a word sits on the tip of the tongue and then, mercifully, stops mattering.
He would like to answer the voice.
He opens something — not his mouth, exactly, more the intention of a mouth — and what comes out, if anything comes out, he cannot hear from in here.
It doesn’t feel like failure.
That’s the strange part, the part he would tell someone if there were a someone left inside to do the telling: it doesn’t feel like loss from this side.

From this side it feels like being extremely, wonderfully warm, lying in a room that smells correct, waiting for a meal that his mother — whose hands these clearly are, whose kitchen this clearly is, two rooms away with the door open — will call him to any moment now.

Somewhere outside this room, if there is an outside, a second voice is saying something with worry folded into it, saying his name in the stretched-out way that means are you there, can you hear me, and some old reflex, some structure built decades before any of this, wants to reach for it, wants to say yes, of course, where else would I be, and for one full second the reaching almost works, almost surfaces, a hand nearly breaking a still pond — and then the smell of saffron gets stronger, mercifully, and he lets it pull him back down, because it is Tuesday, and he is young, and any moment now his mother is going to call him to the table, and there is nowhere in this warm small forever that he would rather be.
CHAPTER FOUR
[BEFORE]
This one I remember in pieces, which is worse, in some ways, than not remembering it at all.
A reconstruction has the mercy of being someone else’s story.
A piece is undeniably yours, and you’re left holding it not knowing what it’s a piece of.
I have said in another book that I was loved, enormously and obviously, by everybody in that apartment, and I am not going to take a word of it back.
I want to put down the other thing beside it, because the two of them lived in the same eight rooms for the whole of my childhood and neither one ever cancelled the other.
My parents did not fight.
I want to be exact about this because people hear “unhappy marriage” and reach for a picture of raised voices and slammed doors, and there were none.

What there was, instead, was silence — a specific, respectful, terrible silence that could settle over the dinner table on the eighth floor of a building in Elahieh and stay there for the whole of a meal, with the radio on low in the kitchen and the Steinway closed in the corner and nobody being anything other than perfectly polite.
My father would pass my mother a dish.
My mother would say thank you.
And underneath the thank-you there was a gravity, a weight in the air of the room, that a child cannot name and cannot fail to feel, and that
I spent years mistaking for the ordinary weather of a household because I had never lived in any other.
I remember it best as a sound, or the absence of one.

I remember being six or seven and sitting between them on a Friday afternoon with a plate in front of me, listening to the clink of a spoon against a bowl, and the refrigerator, and a car going past on the street eight floors down, and understanding — with the strange practical calm of a child — that the quiet had edges, and that I was inside it, and that the polite thing was not to mention that I was.
They were calm.
They were courteous.

They were, in the specific phrase my mother would later use about it, “very civilised with each other,” and I have come to believe that this was the worst of it — that a shout would have been an admission that there was something worth shouting about, and neither of them would give the other that.
I asked her once, an adult asking an adult, on the phone, from a kitchen in Los Angeles, whether she had been unhappy the whole time.
She was quiet long enough that I understood the quiet was the answer.
Then she said, “I loved him.
He loved me.
Those were never the problem, Ali jan.
The problem was that neither of us could find the door out of the room we were sitting in, and after a while you stop looking for it and just arrange the furniture.”

She told me, on that same call, one more thing I’ve turned over many times since — that it was never about money, though my grandfather’s money sat in the middle of that apartment like a fifth person at every meal, and it was never about another woman or another man, and it was never, in thirty years, about anything either of them could have pointed to.
“He had something in him,” she said.
“Some room he couldn’t let anybody into.
Not me, not you boys, not his own mother.
He’d go into it in the middle of a sentence.
And I’d sit there, across the table, and wait, and after a while I stopped waiting, and after a while longer he stopped noticing that I’d stopped.”

I think about that description more than I probably should, because I recognise, in myself, occasionally, the same architecture — the sense of a room in the middle of the house that nobody else is allowed into, and the suspicion, inherited from somewhere, that going into it in the middle of a sentence is simply what a man does.
The marriage ended the spring I was twenty-three, and I was not there for that either.

I was in Van Nuys, in a studio with a window that faced a wall, two years into a country where nobody knew whose son I was, and my mother called on a Friday afternoon, from the kitchen in Elahieh, and said it in a completely level voice, the way she has said every enormous thing she has ever said to me.
“Your father and I are going to stop.
We’ve talked about it.
It’s decided.
He’s going to take a place of his own.” And then, after a pause in which I could hear the refrigerator, the same refrigerator, eleven thousand kilometres away: “Are you eating?”
There was no shouting at the end either.
That should not have surprised me and it did.
My father packed.

That is the whole of what happened, in the physical sense: a man of fifty-two put his shirts and his radio into two suitcases and left an apartment he had lived in for more than twenty years and had never, in any sense that a lawyer would recognise, owned, because the apartment was my mother’s, and had come to her through her father, the way most of what stood in that household had come.
He took nothing that wasn’t his.
My mother said afterwards that she had told him to take anything he wanted and that he had looked at her as if she had suggested he take the walls.
The same month, he left the firm.
My grandfather’s firm, the one he had gone to work for at twenty-three with a stolen jasmine stem still, in some sense, in his hand.
Nobody asked him to.

He simply did not go back after the papers were signed, and when my grandfather — who was eighty-one and would be dead within two years, of a pneumonia that took him in nine days — sent word that the job was his for as long as he wanted it, my father sent word back that he was grateful, and did not go.
I understand this now as the most complete sentence my father ever spoke.
He would not stay in the house.
He would not stay in the job.
He had accepted one gift from that family at twenty-three and he had spent twenty-nine years paying for it, and he was not going to go on paying for it after the reason had gone.
He never worked again.
Not properly.
Not in anything I could have named to a stranger.

He was fifty-two, an engineer who had put lifts into half the towers in the north of the city, and something in him, from that month forward, simply stopped reaching past the front gate of wherever he happened to be sleeping.
I used to think this was grief doing what grief does, temporarily.
I did not understand, until much later, that it was the beginning of a permanent arrangement.
Here is the part that nobody outside our family has ever believed, and I have stopped trying to make them.
They kept talking.
Not occasionally.
Not at weddings.
Every day.

My father, from wherever he was — a rented room in Tehran that was never an address so much as a place to keep a suitcase between flights, or a lawn chair in my aunt’s garden in Irvine, or, later, the house in Mirdamad — sent my mother messages.
Dozens a day.

Hundreds, some days, she told me, holding the phone up to the camera once so I could see the scroll of them, an entire afternoon of a man’s thoughts arriving in a woman’s kitchen one line at a time: a thing he had eaten, a thing on the radio, a complaint about a grocer, a question about her knee, a photograph of a plate.
And she answered.
Not all of them.
Enough.
“He always said he loved me,” she told me, years after, without any weight on it at all.
“He said it in the messages.
He said it on the phone.
And I’d say, Kamran, I know, and I’d mean it, and then I’d ask him whether he’d taken his sugar pills, because what else is there to do with a man like that.”
“Did you love him?” I asked her, because I was thirty-four and had earned it.
“Of course I loved him,” my mother said.
“I still do.
That was never the problem.
I told you what the problem was.”
I don’t know what my father understood about any of this while it was happening.

I have never once heard his side, not from him — he did not discuss it, ever, not with me, not with Amir, not in the years I might have thought to ask before it was too late to ask him anything at all — and so this whole chapter, like the last one, is built from someone else’s memory of him, which means the one person whose interior experience this chapter is actually about is the one person who never gets to speak in it.
That should probably bother me more than it does.
Mostly it just makes me tired, the same specific tired my mother described, the tiredness of trying to hold a shape that keeps being described to you by everyone except the person who lived it.

I was seven, or eight, the last time I remember the three of us in a room together being entirely easy — a birthday, mine, I think, or close to it — and my father brought too much food, the way he always did, plates and plates of it, more than any child’s party required, and my mother let him, and for one afternoon nobody in that room was waiting for anybody.
I did not know, eating cake off a paper plate, that I was watching something at its fullest.
I have gone back to that afternoon more times than I can count, trying to find the exact moment the quiet came in, and I have never found it, because it didn’t come in at a moment.
It came the way water finally gets through — slowly, over years, so that one day you simply notice there is no wall left, and two people sitting very politely on either side of where it stood.
CHAPTER FIVE
[PRESENT]
It took my mother forty minutes to clear my father’s room, and I watched all forty of them on a telephone, the week after the memorial.
I want to put down how that worked, because I think people who have not done it imagine it as simpler, or crueller, than it actually was.
Neither of his sons could get into the country.

My aunts could have gone, and would have, and my mother said no — said it in the level voice, on a call the day after the memorial — because she was there, and she had a key, and because, she said, “I lived with that man’s things for thirty years, Ali jan, I know which drawer he’d have kept anything in.” So she went to Mirdamad with Fatemeh khanom, who had kept that house for my grandmother for twenty years and had kept my father alive in it for two, and she propped her phone against a stack of his shirts on the bed, and she went through the room while I sat on the floor of my own kitchen in Los Angeles at six in the morning and watched.
Half of the forty minutes was her standing still in the doorway, waiting for there to be more.
There wasn’t more.

This was the thing she kept discovering, over and over, opening drawers like each one might correct the last one’s disappointment, and turning to the camera each time with the same small tilt of the head.

A man lives sixty-five years and the room he dies in holds four shirts, two pairs of trousers gone soft at the knee, a pair of reading glasses with one arm reinforced by tape gone amber with age, a blood pressure cuff, a glucose meter with its little lancets in a plastic case, four prescription bottles with names I now know better than I know most poems, and a small wooden box of my grandmother’s — not his, hers, inherited rather than accumulated — containing a string of worn prayer beads and a single photograph of a woman I have only ever known old, young, laughing at something outside the frame.
That was the whole inventory.
I want to be exact about this because I think the exactness is the point: no letters.
No journal.

No box of ticket stubs, no drawer of photographs he’d taken himself, because he had never really taken any — the family album, such as it is, exists almost entirely because other people occasionally remembered to point a camera at him.
No favourite book with a spine cracked in one particular place from being reread.
No cassette, no record, no evidence of a song.
My mother went through everything twice, the second time slower, telling me she’d missed something, and what she found the second time was the same nothing, just more thoroughly confirmed.

Tucked behind the prescription bottles, in the back of the top drawer, she did find one more thing on the second pass that she’d missed the first time — a folded paper receipt, gone soft and nearly transparent with age, and she unfolded it and held it up to the camera and said, “This is yours, I think,” and I made her hold it closer, and it was from a Persian restaurant in Tarzana, California, and it was dated the twenty-second of May, 2015.
I know that date.

I know exactly what evening it belonged to, because it was the evening of the day I graduated, and my father had driven up from Irvine in a car that was not his and sat in a stadium in the San Fernando Valley for four hours in a jacket, and afterwards the three of us ate in a booth in Tarzana with a telephone propped against the sugar so my mother could watch from a kitchen in Elahieh at nine in the morning her time, and my father had insisted on paying and had made a performance of the bill that my brother still does at parties.
There was no note on it, nothing written in any margin, nothing to indicate why it had been kept when literally nothing else had.
I sat there for a long time on the floor of my kitchen looking at a piece of paper on a screen, and my mother, who is not stupid, did not say anything, and let me have it.

I have decided, in the months since, to believe it mattered — that somewhere in that eleven-year-old evening was a meal good enough, or a table full enough, that some small, wordless part of him wanted proof it had happened, even if the rest of him never once mentioned it to anyone.
My mother put it in the wooden box with the beads and the photograph.

It felt, of everything in that room, like the single object closest to an actual answer to the questions I hadn’t been able to answer at the memorial, even though it told me nothing at all — not the dish, not whether he’d enjoyed it.
Just that an evening had occurred, once, in a country he only ever visited, worth this much preservation by accident.
There was a radio.

I should say that, because it felt, for a moment, like it might be the answer — a small clock radio on the nightstand, the kind that has been in every version of every room he ever slept in as long as I can remember, in Elahieh and in Irvine and in Mirdamad.
My mother turned it on, absurdly, because I asked her to, as if it would tell me something, as if the last station he’d left it on would be a message.
It was set to nothing in particular.

Static and a sports call-in show, a stranger arguing about a match, and I sat on a kitchen floor eleven thousand kilometres away listening to a dead man’s radio playing a stranger’s opinion about a game he had probably never once cared about, and I laughed, once, badly, the kind of laugh that’s really a different thing wearing a laugh’s clothes.
My mother sat on the edge of the bed for a while after that.
Long enough that the light in the room changed colour on my screen without either of us noticing it happening.

I keep coming back to something a friend said to me once, about a different loss, years ago — that grief is partly the work of sorting a person’s things into keep and let go, and that the sorting itself is a kind of mercy, because it gives your hands something honest to do while the rest of you catches up.

I had been almost looking forward to that, I think, in the ugly, practical corner of the mind that plans logistics even during catastrophe, until it became clear that my hands were not going to be allowed anywhere near it.
I had pictured myself holding some object of his — a watch, a pen, a specific shirt — turning it over, deciding it mattered, keeping it.
There was nothing to sort.
Nothing sat in the keep pile because there was, essentially, no pile.
My mother put the wooden box in her bag, with the beads and the photograph and the receipt, and said, “This is yours.
I’ll keep it until,” and did not finish the sentence, because neither of us knows what the until is, and I understood, watching her zip the bag, that I wasn’t being handed a piece of my father.
I was being handed a piece of his mother, because it was the only object in that entire room that had clearly, undeniably, been loved by somebody once.
He had, somewhere in the last fourteen years, become a man who did not accumulate.
Not sentimentally, not materially, not in any direction I could find.
He ate his meals outside the house and left no restaurant receipts, except one.
He wore his clothes until they gave out and did not replace them with anything that expressed a preference.
He watched a television that was, as far as I could tell, never once tuned by him to something he’d chosen, only ever left running, company more than entertainment.

Somewhere in the wreckage of the marriage and the leaving of the firm and the years in his sisters’ spare rooms and the return to his mother’s house and the slow years after her death, he had apparently made a decision — not announced, not discussed, maybe not even conscious — to want less and less, on purpose or not, until there was almost nothing left in the room to prove he’d wanted anything at all.

I sat with the phone in my hand and thought about the dervishes, the ones you see spinning in the old films, arms out, one palm up and one down, and how the whole point of the turning, as I understood it, was to arrive eventually at nothing — no possessions, no attachments, nothing left to carry into whatever comes after.
I don’t think my father was trying to become a mystic.

I think he was just tired, in a specific, un-noble way that has nothing to do with enlightenment, and tired people stop collecting things because collecting requires believing there will be a future in which the thing matters.
She came into the kitchen while my mother was still on the screen, and stood behind me, and looked at the four shirts on the bed, and did not say anything until my mother had said goodbye.
Then she said something I’ve kept with me since: “Maybe that’s not emptiness.
Maybe that’s just a man who’d already given away everything that could be given, a long time before this room.” I didn’t know, at the time, whether I believed her.
I think I believe her more now, months later, than I did sitting on that floor with the evidence of his absence on a screen the size of my hand.
But it looked, from where I was sitting, almost the same.
A room emptied down to almost nothing.
A man who left this world exactly as unencumbered as the ones who spend a lifetime trying to arrive there on purpose.

My mother turned off the radio mid-argument, and picked up the phone, and did not point it back into the room again before she closed the door, because there was, at that point, genuinely nothing left in it to look at.
CHAPTER SIX
[BEFORE]

My grandmother’s house had a smell that met you at the gate, before you’d even crossed the little courtyard off the street in Mirdamad — onion browning slow, always slow, because she believed anything browned quickly was being disrespected — and under that, rosewater, and under that, something mineral and old that I have never smelled anywhere since and would not be able to name if my life depended on it.
I think it was just the smell of a house that had been lived in by one family for forty years without interruption.
Some houses smell like that.
Most don’t get the chance.

Katayoun was a small, imprecise, ferociously exact woman — imprecise in the sense that she never once measured an ingredient in her life, exact in the sense that the food came out the same, to the mouth, every single time.

She ran that kitchen the way some women run companies, and my father, her only son, was both her favourite employee and her favourite critic, and their entire relationship, as far as I ever witnessed it, was conducted through food and insult in roughly equal measure.
He would tell her the rice was slightly overcooked.
She would tell him he’d said the same thing every week for thirty years and had somehow, in thirty years, never once refused a second plate.
He would take the second plate to prove her wrong about something, though I was never clear on what.

She had buried her husband — my grandfather Abbas, who had come up from the south of the city with her when my father was a boy and never once, in the north, stopped being a man from the south — the year I turned nine, after two years of a disappearing that nobody in that family ever once gave its name.
I was nine and I stopped speaking for six weeks, which is another book, and my grandmother, who was sixty-two and had just watched her husband forget her face, did not stop doing anything.
She cooked.
That was her answer to it.

She cooked for the seventh day and the fortieth and for every Friday after, and she narrated the market to anyone in earshot the moment she returned from it — which vendor had tried to shortchange her, which one had given her an extra handful of herbs “because he knows I have grandsons to feed,” which tomatoes were an insult to the very idea of a tomato.

My father inherited this narrating impulse whole, unmodified, down to the cadence, and I understood only much later, hearing him complain about a grocer on a Friday phone call decades after, that I wasn’t hearing my father’s voice so much as hers, still running, still complaining, carried forward inside him like a second heartbeat.

I have one particular holiday memory of that house that I return to often, more than any single photograph — a Nowruz gathering when I was perhaps ten, the whole extended family crowded into rooms that were never designed to hold that many people at once, my grandmother directing the chaos from the kitchen like a small, fierce general, my father running food out to the table in relays, my mother sitting where she had been placed with a plate she did not want and a smile she had decided on in the car, everyone talking over everyone else in the specific joyful noise that only happens when a family briefly forgets to be careful with each other.

I remember my father, that night, pulling me aside near the end of the evening, slightly out of breath from carrying dishes, and saying, with an intensity that surprised me even then, “This is the whole thing, you understand?
This right here.
Everything else is just waiting for this.” I did not understand what he meant at ten years old.

I understand it now as close to a thesis statement for his entire life — that the noise and crowding and excess of that one house, on that one night, was the fullest expression he ever found of what he wanted from the world, and that everything after her death was, in some sense, an ongoing failure to recreate a room that could no longer exist without her in it.

This was the table where the spoon-swatting happened, the same story from a few chapters back, and I want to say plainly here what I only understood much later: that table was the last place my father was ever fully, unguardedly himself in front of other people.
Not with my mother, not with me, not with anyone he met afterwards in any country.
Only there, only with her, only over food that had been “disrespected” by being browned too quickly.
He went back to her the autumn I was thirty-three.

He had spent the better part of a decade by then being a man without an address — a room in Tehran, a spare bedroom in Irvine, a suitcase that was never fully unpacked in either — and my grandmother was eighty-six and had begun, the way old bodies do, to fail slowly, nothing anyone could name as a single illness, just a gradual, cumulative tiredness that took a little more of her every season, until the woman who had run that kitchen for fifty years could no longer stand at her own stove for more than a few minutes at a time.

And my father, who was in California that summer, in his sister’s garden, in a lawn chair, arguing with Mr Rostami about the price of melons, got on a plane in October and went home to Mirdamad, and did not come back.
He did not send her anywhere.

I want to say this plainly, because I think it is the single most important fact in this entire chapter: he did not hire a nurse, did not move her to a facility, did not so much as ask Farah or Shirin to fly over and share the load in any sustained way, though both of them offered and one of them came, for a month, and was sent home.
He simply became her nurse, in addition to being her son, without ever once discussing that this was what he was doing.

He fed her, in the end, by hand — small spoonfuls of the same soups she’d taught him to make, sitting on the edge of her bed for what Fatemeh khanom told my mother were sometimes hours at a stretch, patient in a way none of us had ever seen him be with anyone else, patient in a way I don’t think he had it in him to be with a wife, or with his own sons on our more difficult days, or with himself.
He read to her, in the evenings, from newspapers she could no longer focus on herself, narrating the world back to her the same way she’d once narrated the market to him.
He slept, for the better part of her last year, in a chair pulled up beside her bed rather than in his own room down the hall, close enough to hear if her breathing changed in the night.
I did not witness any of this.
I want that on the record, because a man who builds rooms for a living in which strangers are made to feel they were present at something has to be careful about the difference.
I was in Los Angeles.

I knew it from Friday phone calls in which he said almost nothing about it — “she’s the same, she ate, don’t ask me about it” — and from my mother, who went to that house more often in those two years than she had in the previous twenty, and who told me, in the level voice, that my father tended to his mother with a devotion that bordered on the total erasure of himself.

I have thought, many times since, about the particular cruelty and mercy both folded into that fact: that the one person he ever nursed with his whole undivided attention was his mother, in her final year, in the same house where he himself would spend his own final months being nursed by a housekeeper, and an ex-wife, and two sons on a telephone.

He gave her exactly what, two years later, he would not receive back — not because anyone failed him, but because geography and circumstance and a pair of hands had rearranged themselves in the intervening years into something none of us could undo from where we stood.

She died on an ordinary evening in October, in her own bed, in the room she had slept in since my father was a boy, with my father sitting beside her holding her hand, her breathing simply slowing and then stopping over the course of an hour that he described to me only once, on the phone, weeks afterwards, in one of the only unguarded sentences I ever got out of him about any of this: “She looked like she was deciding something.
Not afraid.
Deciding.” There was no final crisis, no ambulance, no argument about what more could be done.

There was only a son who had spent two years making himself entirely available to one long goodbye, and a mother who, having buried a husband and outlasted almost everyone she had ever cooked for, got to leave the world in the one room and the one set of arms she’d have chosen if anyone had thought to ask her.
She was eighty-eight.
I want the number here, because it is the only kind of fact about that death that I actually possess.

I did not fly back for the burial, because I could not, and I remember almost nothing about the week after except that I did not know what to say on the phone to a grown man standing in his dead mother’s kitchen, and said nothing, and regretted the nothing for years afterwards without ever finding the sentence that should have filled it.

Fatemeh khanom told my mother that he stood in that kitchen on the third or fourth day holding one of her spice tins, not doing anything with it, just holding it, turning it slowly in his hands the way you’d hold something you were afraid of dropping and also afraid of setting down.
He did not change anything.

Not the following week, not the following year, not ever, as far as I could tell from the video calls in which Fatemeh khanom occasionally, at my request, turned the phone around and walked it through the house.
Her room stayed her room.
Her spice tins stayed in the order she’d kept them, an order that made sense to no one but her and that he preserved anyway, as if rearranging them would be a second death on top of the first.

The chair she’d always sat in stayed empty and occupied at the same time, the way certain chairs do in certain houses, everyone unconsciously leaving it alone at dinner even when there were guests and not enough seats.

The chair beside her bed, the one he’d slept in for a year, stayed pulled up close to the mattress for the rest of his life, as if some part of him was still keeping the vigil long after there was no one left to keep it for.

I think, if I’m honest, that this is the chapter where he actually died — not the one at the end of this book, but this one, quietly, two years earlier, in a way that took the rest of his life to finish arriving.

The marriage had already taken something from him, but a marriage ending, however politely, still leaves you technically free to go build something else somewhere else, and for a decade he had at least gone back and forth across an ocean pretending that he might.
His mother’s death, and the two years of devotion that preceded it, took the last argument he had for going anywhere.
The house in Mirdamad had been the place he retreated to when everything else was gone.

Once she was gone too, the house stopped being a retreat and became, simply, the only place left, because it was the only place where enough of her remained that leaving would have felt like abandoning her twice — and because he had spent two years pouring every remaining ounce of himself into keeping her comfortable in that specific set of rooms, which meant the rooms themselves had absorbed something of that devotion and would not easily let it go.
The sorrow that moved into that house after she died never really moved back out.
I don’t say this as a figure of speech.

I mean that in the calls afterwards there was a particular quality to the air in certain rooms — her bedroom especially, but the kitchen too, and the chair by the window where she used to sit — a heaviness I could see on a screen, that had nothing to do with dust or disuse and everything to do with a grief that had simply never been given anywhere else to go.
He did not talk about her often.
He did not need to.

The house talked about her constantly, in the arrangement of tins, in the chair no one sat in, in the particular slow, careful way he still, two years later, entered her old room, as if the door itself required a kind of respect he extended to nothing else in his life.
He got quieter after that.

Not overnight — I want to be careful not to make this sound like a single dramatic year — but steadily, the way a room gets darker as the sun goes down, so gradually that you can be sitting in it the whole time and only notice the dark once you try to read something and can’t.
He stopped, around then, doing things that had nothing to do with anyone else’s convenience.

He’d always liked outside food, but now the taking of a meal outside the house became less an appetite than an errand — somewhere to go that required no explanation, no company, no risk of a conversation heavier than ordering.

He kept the radio on, always, in every room, at a volume too low to actually listen to, which I understand now, and did not understand then, as a man arranging the sound of other voices around himself so the silence of the house would have something to compete with.
And I called less than I should have, in those years.
I told myself it was the time difference, and work, and the ordinary momentum of a life being built somewhere else.
Some of that was true.

Some of it, if I’m honest in the way this book keeps demanding I be honest, was that a call to him in that house had started to feel like a call to a museum where the one exhibit still breathing was quietly, patiently, waiting to join the rest of the collection.
CHAPTER SEVEN
[BEFORE — HUMOUR]
This is one of the only chapters in this book I don’t have to reconstruct from anyone else’s memory.
I was there.
Amir was there.

It remains, to this day, the single funniest afternoon of my adult life, and I make no apology for putting a chapter like this in a book about grief, because he would have been furious with me if I hadn’t.

It started because my father had, somewhere in his early fifties, in the first of the years he spent going back and forth between a room in Tehran and his sisters’ spare bedrooms in Irvine, developed an almost religious devotion to a massage parlour in a strip mall on Westwood Boulevard — a cramped, over-lit storefront between a pharmacy and a place that sold saffron by the gram, with a laminated price list taped to the window and a curtain instead of a door for the back room, run by a heavyset, no-nonsense woman from Rasht named Parvin who had, according to my father, “hands like a wrestler and the patience of a saint, which is the only correct combination for this work.” He went weekly, whenever he was in the country, which meant a seventy-minute drive up the 405 in my aunt’s car for a forty-minute massage.
He spoke of Parvin the way other men speak of a favourite football team — total loyalty, occasional public complaint, no possibility of switching allegiance.
The walk from the car park was itself a small performance, and I want to include it because Amir and I still, to this day, occasionally re-enact it for each other unprompted.

Our father set a pace that was somehow both leisurely and urgent, stopping twice to greet shopkeepers by name, once to critique a display of fruit outside the grocer’s that he had no intention of buying (“who arranges melons like this, an animal?”), and once, memorably, to have a fully separate argument with a man selling roasted corn from a cart about whether the corn had been sitting too long, an argument that ended, as they nearly all did, with my father buying two ears anyway and eating them both before we’d even reached Parvin’s door.
Parvin’s shop itself deserves its own small description, because it was, in its way, as much a monument to my father’s particular tastes as the kebab stalls or the bakery ever were.

The front room held two plastic chairs, a low table stacked with outdated Persian magazines nobody read, and a hand-lettered price list that Parvin updated herself in a marker that had clearly been rewritten over the same cardboard so many times the old prices ghosted through beneath the new ones.

There was a small radio behind the counter, always on, always tuned to the same Persian station from Encino that my father kept on in every room of my aunt’s house, and I remember noticing, the first time we visited, that this alone might explain years of loyalty better than any massage technique could — that he had found, in a strip mall in Westwood, one more room that sounded exactly like home.

Amir had come from Toronto that spring for four nights, the second of only two times we saw each other in eleven years, and our father had driven up from Irvine for two of them, and treated the overlap like a holiday, and on the second day he announced, over breakfast, with the tone of a man conferring an honour, that he was taking us to Parvin’s.
We should have been suspicious of his enthusiasm.
We were not.
The back room, it turned out, had exactly one table.
My father had not mentioned this.

What this meant, practically, was that Amir and I sat on two plastic chairs against the wall, drinking bitter tea from paper cups, while our father went first, “since I made the introduction,” and Parvin worked on him behind a curtain thin enough that we could hear absolutely everything and see, through a gap where the fabric didn’t quite meet the wall, an alarming quantity of him.
He narrated the entire massage.
Not to us — to Parvin, at volume, as though she were a colleague he was training rather than a professional he was paying.
“There.

There, exactly, don’t be shy about it, my mother used to hit harder than that with a spoon and I survived.” Parvin, who I would come to understand had heard every version of this speech for years, did not slow down or speed up or acknowledge the review in any way, which somehow made it funnier, the two of them locked in a routine so old it had stopped requiring either party to actually respond to the other.
At some point — Amir swears it was eleven minutes in, I maintain it was closer to fifteen, this remains a genuine unresolved dispute between us — our father began to snore.
Loudly.
Mid-instruction.

He had been in the process of telling Parvin that his left shoulder “held all his regrets” when the sentence simply stopped, replaced by a snore so enormous and unselfconscious that Amir had to put his paper cup down before he spilled it laughing, and Parvin, without missing a beat, without so much as glancing toward us, said, through the curtain, in the flattest voice I have ever heard a human being produce, “He does this every week.
I am used to it now.
He wakes up insulted regardless of what I have done.”
He did wake up insulted.
He woke, roughly twenty minutes later, sat halfway up on the table, looked around as if trying to locate the exact person responsible, and announced, to no one and everyone, “Zahremar!

Why did nobody wake me, I came here for a massage, not a coma” — and then, without any transition at all, accused Parvin of having gone soft on his shoulder specifically because he’d fallen asleep and couldn’t defend it, refused to pay the listed price because he claimed the nap portion of the session should be discounted, negotiated for what felt like a genuinely unreasonable length of time over what amounted to less than the cost of a modest lunch, in a country where nobody negotiates, lost the negotiation completely, as he always did, and then — as he always did — tipped Parvin nearly double the difference on his way out, muttering something about her hands and her patience, loud enough that she’d hear it, quiet enough that he could pretend, if asked, that he hadn’t meant her to.
Amir went next.
I went last.

By the time it was my turn, Parvin had clearly decided that the entire family shared whatever affliction had produced my father, and treated me with the specific gentleness people reserve for someone they’ve already forgiven in advance for something they haven’t done yet.
She took my right hand, at one point, and turned it over, and looked at the palm, and looked at me, and said nothing about it at all, and went back to work, and I have loved her for that ever since.

She asked, halfway through, without any particular emotion in her voice, whether we were “always like this,” and I said yes, and she nodded slowly, as if this confirmed a theory she’d been developing over the better part of seven years, and did not say another word.

Afterwards, walking back to the car, my father in front, one hand pressed theatrically to the shoulder that “held all his regrets,” complaining the whole way that Parvin had “definitely gone soft on purpose, out of spite, because I fell asleep and she took it personally” — Amir looked at me and mouthed, silently, over our father’s head: he tipped her double.
And I mouthed back, because it was true and because it was the whole of him in one sentence: of course he did.
I think about that walk more than almost anything else from those years.
Not because it was important.
Because it wasn’t.

It was small, and loud, and slightly ridiculous, and utterly, recognisably him — a man who would negotiate you down to nothing and then quietly overpay out of some private accounting system only he understood, who would insult a service he loved so completely he drove seventy minutes each way for it, who fell asleep mid-complaint and considered the complaint unfinished business rather than let sleep have the last word.

I did not know, walking to the car that day, laughing at my brother’s silent joke behind our father’s back, that I was collecting one of the only afternoons I would ever be able to answer for, later, when someone asked me what he was like.
Not his favourite song.
Not his favourite food, though God knows I could have answered that one too, eventually, if anyone had ever asked me about outside food and given me an hour.
But this — a man narrating his own massage to a woman who’d stopped listening years ago, snoring through his own complaint, overpaying to make up for a fight he’d started and lost on purpose.
If someone had asked me that day at the memorial what he was like, instead of what he liked, I would have had an answer ready in half a second.
Nobody asked me that.
CHAPTER EIGHT
[INTERIOR II]

There is a phone ringing, or there was, or there will be — the order of things has stopped being something he can rely on, the way you can no longer rely on a floor once you know it might, at any point, simply not be there.
A face is on the other side of it.
He knows the face is a good face, a face that belongs to him in the particular way certain faces do, the way a hand belongs to an arm without needing to be introduced to it.

The face is saying something with its mouth shaped around news, around a word that might be moved or might be a name or might be remember — they have started, lately, to sound almost the same to him, three shapes of hope aimed in his direction, and he receives the hope even when the specific cargo of it slides off him like water off something no longer able to hold water.
He would like to say the correct thing back.

There is, somewhere behind where his voice used to live, an old and enormous willingness to be pleased for whatever this is — a woman’s name, a flat with light in it, a room with a wall of names on it that strangers will stand in front of for four minutes — and the willingness is real, the willingness is possibly the last fully intact thing in the whole structure, but it has nowhere left to go.

It sits in his chest and glows and cannot get out through the door that used to be his mouth, because the door, lately, only opens onto other rooms — his mother’s kitchen, a spoon, a curtain with a gap in it, a woman’s laugh from a photograph he does not remember being shown but somehow already knows.
Two faces are folding into each other now, the way steam folds into more steam.
One of them is small and frowning and standing in a doorway in a thin jacket in Esfand, refusing a coat.
One of them is older, holding a phone toward him like an offering, with the same frown.
He cannot, if his life depended on it — and in some sense it does, in some sense this is exactly what his life now depends on — locate the line between them.
He is not frightened by this.
That is the part no one watching from outside could possibly guess: from in here, the folding doesn’t feel like losing anyone.
It feels like everyone finally being close enough to touch at once.
Somewhere, underneath everything, a radio he cannot remember is turned to a station he cannot name, arguing quietly about a game whose rules he no longer needs.
He lets it hold the silence for him, the way it always has, the way it was always, without his ever once explaining it to anyone, doing exactly that job.
The face on the phone says his name.

It says it twice, slowly, stretched a little long at the end, the way he used to say the boy’s, buying himself a second — though which of them is doing the buying, now, and which is the boy, he could not say, and it doesn’t matter half as much as the fact that it is being said at all, that somewhere, still, someone is saying his name like it’s worth the extra second.
He cannot answer.
He is fairly sure, in the dim mechanical way he is sure of anything now, that something in his face is trying to.
He hopes, in the last language he has left for hoping, that this is somehow enough.
That the trying shows.
CHAPTER NINE
[BEFORE]

I left the spring I was twenty-one, at ten past four in the morning, from an airport where nobody in my family was crying, and I have written elsewhere about the queue and the bag and the man who came to see me off with bread in a plastic bag, and I am not going to write it again.
My father was not at the airport.
I want to be careful about how that is read, because there is a version of this book in which that is a cruelty and it was not one.

He had said goodbye the night before, in the apartment, at the door, with one hand raised, not waving so much as simply held up, as if checking the weather, and had then gone into his room and shut the door, and my mother had looked at the door and then at me and said nothing, and I understood that this was the arrangement, and that the arrangement was the best he had.
My father did not ask me to stay.
I used to think this meant he didn’t mind.

It took me a long time to understand it might have meant the opposite — that a man who had spent nearly three decades sitting in a polite silence across a table from a woman he loved had developed a policy, somewhere along the way, of never asking anyone for anything he suspected they might refuse.
The country he stayed in was not one I could go back to.

I won’t turn this book into a history lesson about why — that isn’t the story I’m telling, and he would have hated me turning his last years into a current-events segment, and the private part of the reason lives in two other books and in the way my right hand closes — but I’ll say plainly that from the day I landed in Los Angeles there was no version of a plane ticket in the other direction that ended with me leaving again on schedule, and that everyone in my family knew it, and that nobody ever once said it at a dinner table.

She asked me once, early, gently, whether it was really true, whether there was really no way, and I remember not having a clean answer, because the true answer was something like: there is always a way, and every one of them ends in a room I have already been in once.
So the distance was not a thing we managed.
It was a thing we lived inside, all of us, from the first week.
And then, two years in, the marriage ended, and my father did the thing that nobody in the family had predicted, which was that he came to me.
Not to live.

He could not have lived with me; I had a studio in Van Nuys with a window that faced a wall, and then a one-bedroom in Frogtown with a lemon tree that belonged to the building, and there was never, in any of the places I have rented in this country, a second room.
He came to his sisters.

Farah and Shirin had been in Orange County since before I could walk, a house and a condominium ten minutes apart in a part of Irvine where every third mailbox has a name I could pronounce, and my father — who had a blue passport in a drawer from a decade earlier that he had never once used for anything but a stamp — got on a plane the summer after the divorce and came and stayed in Farah’s spare room for four months.
And then went back.
And then came again, in the spring, for five.
And then went back.
That was the rhythm of the next nine years.

Months at a time in a lawn chair in Irvine, and then months at a time in a rented room in Tehran that he described so little that I could not have drawn it for you, and the ocean in between, crossed and recrossed by a man who had, as far as I could tell, no particular reason to be on either side of it except that his sons were on one and his mother was on the other.
I drove down most Sundays when he was here.
Seventy minutes on the 405 in a car I had owned for four months and then a car I had owned for four years.

I would find him in the garden, in the same chair, with the radio on the table beside him tuned to the station from Encino, and a plate of something on his knee, and Mr Rostami from three doors down in the other chair, and the two of them would be in the middle of an argument about the moral collapse of the neighbourhood that had, I gathered, been running continuously since the previous Sunday.
He would look up when I came through the gate and say, “Ah.
The engineer,” which was a joke, because I was not one and he was, and then he would tell me to sit down, and ask me if I had eaten, and not wait for the answer.
I want to put down what those Sundays were actually like, because there is a version of a divorced father in a spare room that gets told and it is either pathos or comedy and mine was neither.

It was a man of fifty-five, and then sixty, in a garden in Southern California with a plate of fruit, in a country whose language he spoke well enough to insult a parking attendant and not well enough to make a friend, being visited by a son who lived in a city forty miles away and could not fit him in it.
We did not talk about the divorce.
We did not talk about my mother, except that he would ask, every Sunday, whether I had spoken to her, and I would say yes, and he would nod, and that was the whole of it.
We did not talk about the job he had walked away from or the fact that he had not, in the years since, found another one.
We talked about food.
We talked about the radio.

We talked, at enormous length, about the parking situation at my aunt Shirin’s complex, where he slept when Farah’s spare room was taken, which he regarded as a standing indictment of the moral character of the state of California.

And every Sunday, when I left, he would walk me to the gate, and stand there with one hand raised, the way he had stood at the door in Elahieh, and I would drive back up the 405 in the dark and feel the specific thing you feel when you have spent four hours with a person you love and said nothing to him that either of you will remember.

So we settled, without ever deciding to, into the rhythm that would define the last decade and a half of his life: a call most Fridays, sometimes Saturdays, always roughly the same shape, and a lawn chair in Irvine for a few months a year.
Did you eat.
How is work.
Is it cold there.
Have you spoken to your mother.
Send a picture of the flat.
The calls rarely ran longer than ten minutes, and I used to feel a little guilty about that, as though love should require more sustained attention than a ten-minute check-in could provide.
I understand it differently now.

Ten minutes, every single Friday, for fifteen years, adds up to something much larger than any single long conversation could have been — it adds up to a kind of scaffolding, a structure you don’t notice holding anything up until it’s gone.

He would ask the same four or five questions in roughly the same order nearly every time, and I used to find this repetitive in a mildly irritating way, the way any ritual can feel irritating when you’re young enough to still believe rituals are optional.

I did not yet understand that the repetition was the entire point — that he wasn’t asking because he’d forgotten the answers from the week before, but because asking was how he touched the distance between us, the way you might run your hand along a wall in the dark, not to learn anything new about the wall, just to confirm it was still there.

Somewhere inside that rhythm, for the last four years of it, there lived one running joke he never once let die, and he brought it out nearly every single call like it was fresh material every time: the woman I live with, and the years I had apparently spent failing to marry her.
“Three years,” he’d say, the way other men might announce a batting average, and then, the following winter, “Four.
Four years, and you still haven’t asked her.
What are you waiting for, a written invitation from God himself?

I could be dead by the time you get around to it” — and then, immediately, delighted with his own darkness, he’d laugh at his own line before I could even react to it, with no sound, shoulders going, which on a video call from Mirdamad meant the whole picture shook.

“Cheshmam roshan,” he’d add sometimes, which means, more or less, my eyes are brightened — a phrase people use sincerely when good news arrives, and which he used entirely sarcastically, the way you’d say “wonderful” about something that was very much not wonderful yet.
“I want grandchildren,” he’d say, most calls, some version of it.
“Your brother gave me one and she answers me in English.

You’re taking your time on purpose, I think, just to torture an old man.” I would tell him, every time, that we’d get there, that there was no rush, and he would make a sound of theatrical despair, as if I’d just confirmed his worst fears about the entire younger generation, and then ask what I’d eaten for lunch, subject closed, until the following Friday, when he’d open it again like it had never once been closed at all.
I used to find this mildly exhausting, the way you find any joke exhausting on its four hundredth telling.

I did not understand, then, that he meant every word of it completely, underneath the performance — that the joke was the only shape he had available for a want that large, and that dressing it as a bit was simply how a man like him kept a real hope from sounding like a real hope, in case the real hope didn’t come true in time.
He was not, by nature or by choice, a man of pictures.

I want to say this clearly because I think people who didn’t know him assume, now, that there must be some trove somewhere — a phone full of family photos, a saved folder of video calls — and there isn’t, not really.
He’d pose for one photograph a year if pressed, always the same expression, half-cooperating, and then hand the phone back like he’d done you a favour he didn’t fully understand the point of.

Video calls made him visibly uncomfortable in a way I never got to the bottom of; he’d hold the phone too close or too far, ask “can you see me” four times in a single call, and seem relieved when it ended.
What I have instead — what I will have, now, for the rest of my life, in place of a father — is voice messages.
Dozens of them, saved without any real system, sent at odd hours because he never fully adjusted to the time difference in either direction and didn’t seem to think it mattered.
Some are thirty seconds.

Some run four or five minutes, him talking through some minor frustration about a neighbour or a delivery or the price of something, his voice doing the thing it always did when he was truly comfortable — sliding into a kind of run-on grumbling that required no response, because it wasn’t really a question, it was company, the audio version of the radio he kept on in every room.
I did not know, sending back a thirty-second reply between meetings, in the years when he was still fully himself, that I was building the only archive I would ever have of him.
If I had known, I think I would have asked him more.

I think I would have asked him, directly, on one of those ordinary Friday calls, what song he’d want played at the end of things, and he would have laughed at me for asking something so morbid, and made a joke instead, and I would have let him, because that was easier for both of us, and because neither of us believed, on any of those ordinary Fridays, that there was a deadline attached to the question.
There wasn’t supposed to be a deadline.
That’s the part I keep returning to.
