We had got so used to the rhythm of the calls that the rhythm itself started to feel like a kind of permanence — as if a relationship conducted entirely in thirty-second increments, across a distance neither of us could close from my side, might simply go on that way forever, a low, steady hum in the background of two separate lives, requiring nothing further from either of us but the next Friday.
CHAPTER TEN
[BEFORE — HUMOUR]
Not everything from those years was distance and static.

Some of it was food, always food, and some of it was rage — his rage, specifically, a magnificent, disproportionate, entirely theatrical rage that could be summoned by almost nothing and burned itself out almost as fast as it arrived, leaving behind no residue except a story his sons would still be telling each other for the rest of their lives.
On the food: he had, by his sixties, refined his devotion to eating outside the house into something closer to a personal cosmology.

There were, in his accounting, exactly three trustworthy kebab stalls in the whole of Mirdamad, and he could tell you, unprompted, at length, on a Friday phone call, precisely why the fourth one — the one everyone else seemed to like — was a fraud.
“They rush the fire,” he told me once, with the gravity of a man delivering a verdict in a murder trial.
“You cannot rush the fire.

The fire knows if you rush it, and it takes its revenge on you later, in your stomach, at three in the morning.” He ordered, always, more than any single person could eat, on the stated theory that “a good meal deserves witnesses, even if the witnesses are just what’s left on the plate tomorrow,” and he would eat the leftovers the next day with the same ceremony as the original meal, sometimes greater ceremony, as if the dish had improved overnight through sheer patience.

That he was a diabetic, and had been told so by three doctors on two continents, entered into this cosmology only as a kind of weather — something to be complained about, never something to be obeyed.

There was a stretch of about two years, after his mother died, when he became intensely obsessed with a bakery in the south of the city — in the neighbourhood where he had been born and where his own father had repaired sewing machines for forty years — that sold a particular kind of bread he claimed, with no evidence I was ever able to verify, my grandfather Abbas had loved above all other breads.

He would take a bus — an actual bus, forty minutes south, a genuine inconvenience for a man who otherwise organised his entire life around minimising inconvenience — twice a week, specifically for this bread, and would return with far more of it than any household of one could reasonably consume, and would then complain, without fail, on the phone, that the bakery had “changed something, I don’t know what, but it’s not the same as last week,” and would go back anyway the following Tuesday to check again.
Amir once asked him, reasonably, on a three-way call, why he kept going if it disappointed him every time.

My father looked at the phone like the question itself was the disappointing thing, and said, “Because it might be right this time,” and that, Amir still says, is as close as our father ever came to a personal philosophy, delivered entirely by accident, about a loaf of bread.
The rage was a different art form entirely, and it required almost no provocation.

Amir still tells the story — better than I do, admittedly, because he was in the car and I was too small to be anywhere but the back seat — of the Great Parking Incident, in which our father spent nearly twenty minutes circling the same three streets in Elahieh, growing steadily, audibly furious at a stranger’s car parked “at an angle only a criminal would choose,”

muttering “bi-fahm” — roughly, this person has no sense — under his breath every time he passed it again, a car that was, by any reasonable measure, parked perfectly normally, slightly crooked at most, and which our father nonetheless treated as a personal referendum on the moral collapse of the entire neighbourhood.
He did not confront the car’s owner.
He never once, in any version of this story I’ve heard, actually did anything about the source of his fury.

He simply circled, and narrated, and circled, building an entire case in his head against a stranger who would never know the trial had taken place, and then, having found parking eventually, walked into the apartment and asked what was for dinner in a completely normal, entirely recovered voice, as if the last twenty minutes had happened to somebody else.
This was, more or less, the shape of every outburst, in every country.

Something small — a delivery five minutes late, a television remote with a dead battery he insisted was “sabotage,” a grocer on Westwood who’d apparently shortchanged him by an amount neither Amir nor I could ever get him to specify — would ignite him completely, briefly, gloriously, and then vanish almost as fast as it arrived, leaving him calm, occasionally even cheerful, while the rest of us were still catching our breath from the performance.

One entry from “Baba’s Grievances” that Amir and I still quote to each other, word for word, involved an entire afternoon in Irvine he spent convinced that a new neighbour in my aunt Shirin’s complex was deliberately timing their laundry to interfere with his afternoon nap, based on evidence that amounted to the sound of a washing machine occurring, on two separate occasions, within an hour of when he usually lay down.

He drafted, in his head, an entire imagined confrontation with this neighbour, rehearsed portions of it out loud to me over a Sunday lunch, refined the wording of his complaint — in a language he did not speak well enough to deliver it in — over the course of several days, and then, when he finally encountered the neighbour by chance in the car park, said nothing at all beyond a polite nod, and came back in vaguely disappointed in himself for having missed the opportunity, already beginning to draft, my aunt said, an even better version of the speech for next time.
I used to find this exhausting, when I was younger and living under his roof and unable to simply leave the room when the weather turned.

I understand it differently now, from a distance both geographic and temporal — now that I have, myself, discovered the particular fury a man can summon over a dropped glass or a missed exit on the 110, a fury that has nothing to do with the glass or the exit and everything to do with some older, unrelated pressure finally finding a small enough door to escape through.
I think his rages were never really about parking, or remotes, or grocers.

I think they were the pressure of an entire unlived life — the marriage he sat inside for thirty years without a word, the firm he walked away from, the ocean he crossed and recrossed for nine years without ever landing on either side of it, the house he went back to and never left — finding, every so often, some tiny, safe, ridiculous reason to let a little steam out before sealing itself back up again.

Amir and I, for years, kept a private, uncharitable, deeply affectionate list of “Baba’s Grievances,” updated after every visit and every three-way call, and I still have it, in a message thread between us that runs from a phone I owned in 2013 to the one in my pocket now, a running joke that has quietly become one of the only documents I possess that captures him exactly as he was — not the sad ending, not the silence at the end of the phone, but a man circling a parking spot for twenty minutes over a crime that existed only in his own furious, loving, endlessly particular imagination.
CHAPTER ELEVEN
[PRESENT]
She was thirty seconds into a sentence the first time I understood something about my father that I had spent thirty years failing to understand from the outside.
I should say, before anything else in this chapter, the thing that sits underneath all of it: my father did not get his wish.

I did not marry her, not in the four years he counted against me on every call, and there is no child, and by the time either of those things might have happened, he was already too far into the illness to be told in any way that meant what it should have meant, and then too far gone to be told anything at all, and then gone entirely — which means the man who had spent four years threatening, joking, half-serious and fully serious at once, that he might die before he got to hold a grandchild of mine, turned out to have been telling the exact and literal truth of what would happen, dressed the whole time as a joke so the truth of it wouldn’t have to be looked at directly.
There is no photograph of him holding anyone’s child but his own, and those are nearly forty years old, and in them he is thin.
This is not that chapter.

I want to be honest about that, because a book like this one usually has that chapter — the son becomes a father and understands — and I have read those books and I believe them and they are not available to me.
What I have instead is smaller and, I think, worse.
It was a Tuesday evening in the apartment in Frogtown, about a month after the memorial, and she was telling me something about her day.
Nothing that mattered.

A colleague, a thing that had gone wrong with a delivery, the kind of thing people tell each other at the end of a day not because it is interesting but because it is theirs and they want to hand it to somebody.
And I went somewhere.
I want to describe it exactly, because I have spent my adult life describing rooms for a living and this is the only room I have ever found myself in without having built it.

I was sitting across a table from a woman I love, with a plate in front of me, and the radio on low in the kitchen, and she was talking, and at some point in the middle of her sentence I was no longer there.
Not thinking about anything.
Not upset.
Simply absent, gone into some interior room in the middle of my own head with the door pulled quietly to behind me, while my face went on doing whatever a face does when it is being polite.
And she stopped talking.
And waited.
And after a while — I could not tell you how long, which is the point — she said, gently, with no weight on it at all: “You went somewhere.”
And I said, “Sorry.
I’m here.”
And she said, “I know.
You always come back.
It’s just that I never know how long to wait.”
I sat there with the plate in front of me and the radio going and something in my chest turned over so completely that I had to put my fork down.
Because I knew that sentence.
I had never heard it before in my life and I knew it, the way you know a smell — from the inside, before language.

My mother had said it to me, about him, on the phone, three years ago, from a kitchen in Elahieh, in the level voice: he’d go into it in the middle of a sentence, and I’d sit there across the table and wait, and after a while I stopped waiting.
I had spent years — quietly, mostly without saying so out loud, even to myself — building a private case against him.
Why didn’t he fight for the marriage.
Why didn’t he say the thing, whatever the thing was, to the woman he sent three hundred messages a day for fourteen years.
Why did he sit in that silence for three decades and let it become the weather of the house we grew up in.
Why didn’t he leave the house in Mirdamad after his mother died, why didn’t he call more, ask more, want more, for himself and from me.

I had built this case the way you build a case against anyone you love and don’t understand: from the outside, using only the evidence of what he did and didn’t do, with none of the evidence of what it had cost him to do or not do it.

And here I was, at thirty-seven, in a country I had chosen, in a life I had built with my own two hands out of nothing, sitting across a table from the one person in the world I had let all the way in, doing it.
Doing exactly it.
Going into a room in the middle of a sentence and pulling the door to and leaving somebody on the other side of it to decide how long to wait.
I had not learned it from him.
That is the part I need to be careful about.
Nobody taught me the room.

It was simply there, the way a house has a room in it that nobody uses, and I had lived in it for thirty-seven years without once noticing that it was the same room, in the same place, with the same door, as the one my father had disappeared into across every dinner table of my childhood while my mother passed him a dish and said thank you.
This does not excuse anything.
I want to be careful here, because I think it would be easy, and false, to turn this chapter into a tidy forgiveness — now that I have caught myself doing it, I understand, and so I forgive.
It wasn’t that clean.
I still believe he could have fought harder.
I still believe he let the silence win more territory than it should have been allowed, in that apartment and in that marriage and in that house.
Recognising the room did not hand me an excuse on his behalf.
There was a second moment, weeks later, that sharpened this rather than resolved it.

She had gone to bed and I was standing in the kitchen at midnight with the radio on low, and I noticed that I had been standing there for some time, and that I had turned the radio on without deciding to, and that the volume was set at exactly the level at which you cannot actually hear what is being said, only that something is — and I stood very still with my hand on the counter and understood that I was not listening to the radio.
I was arranging the sound of other voices around myself so that the silence of the apartment would have something to compete with.

I had watched him do it in every room he ever slept in, on two continents, for thirty years, and had found it mildly eccentric, and I had never once, until that midnight, asked what the silence was that needed competing with.

What it handed me, instead of forgiveness, was a question I had never once thought to ask, in all the years I still had access to him to ask it: not why didn’t you do more, but what was it like in there?

What did it feel like, sitting at that table, in the middle of a sentence, with the door pulled to and a woman on the other side of it deciding how long to wait, and no way — no vocabulary, no permission, no door — to tell her that you had not gone anywhere on purpose, that you were in there wanting to come out, that the wanting was possibly the last intact thing in the whole structure?
I will never get to ask him that question.

I understand, now, standing in my own dark kitchen with my hand on the counter and the radio murmuring about nothing, that I am the only one left who will ever be able to guess at the answer, and that the guessing is going to have to serve as the conversation we never had.
I turned the radio off.

I stood there a while longer anyway, in the actual silence, because some other part of me — some very old part, I think, some part that had been waiting thirty years for exactly this — needed a few more minutes in that kitchen, understanding, finally, far too late to do anything useful with it, a man I had spent my whole life almost knowing.
Then I went in and woke her up, and told her that when I go somewhere, she should not wait, she should say my name, and that I would come.
It is the only instruction I have ever been able to give anyone about the room.
I do not know whether my father ever had it to give.
I think, if he had, he would have given it to my mother thirty years ago, and this would be a different book, and I would be a different man, and I would not be writing this in the dark.
CHAPTER TWELVE
[BEFORE]

The call came on a Tuesday, which I remember only because I have since developed an irrational distrust of Tuesdays, the way some people distrust a particular street corner after something happens there once.

It was my mother, and she did the thing we’d both learned to do over years of long-distance bad news, which is to say the small true fact first, plainly, before either of us could dress it up into something softer.
“Your father fell,” she said.
“In the bathroom.
He’s all right.
He’s not all right.
Fatemeh khanom found him.”
And then she told me how, in the level voice, in the order it had happened, because she knows that I build rooms for a living and cannot bear to be given the second wall first.

Fatemeh khanom had come in the morning, the way she came every morning, with the key she had had for twenty years, and the house door had been locked from the inside with the chain on, which it never was, because he never used the chain.
She had knocked.
She had rung.

She had stood in the courtyard and called his name through the door in the stretched-out way that means are you there, can you hear me, for what she told my mother was ten minutes and was probably four.

And then she had gone and got the neighbour and his son, and the two of them had put a shoulder to the door until the chain came out of the frame, and she had gone through the house calling his name, and found him on the floor of the bathroom, between the toilet and the wall, where he had been since some hour of the night that nobody would ever establish, in his own piss, with his glasses under the sink and one arm at an angle that was wrong, entirely conscious, and — this is the detail my mother gave me last, and that I have thought about more than any other — apologising.
To Fatemeh khanom.
For the state of the floor.
I was sitting at my desk in Frogtown when she told me this, with a plan of a room on the screen in front of me, and I did not feel the thing I expected to feel.
I had imagined, in whatever idle way you imagine bad news before it arrives, that a call like this would land as a single blow.
Instead it landed the way water finds a crack — quietly, almost gently, and then didn’t stop, spreading backwards through months of Friday calls I now had to look at differently.
The balance he’d lost, once, twice, on the stairs, that he’d mentioned as a joke about the stairs.
The sugar readings he had stopped reporting because I had stopped asking.
The story about the grocer he’d told me twice in the same call, each time as if it were new.

The morning he couldn’t find the word for “kettle” and covered it, with impressive speed, by simply pointing the phone at it and saying “that thing, you know the thing,” and none of us had thought much of it, because everyone forgets a word sometimes, because we had all, without meaning to, been quietly editing the early evidence into something explainable.
Amir called me an hour later, from his own kitchen forty minutes away, because my mother had called him second and he had needed the hour.
He asked what I wanted to do.

This is the question that distance turns into its own particular cruelty — not “what do you feel,” but “what do you want to do,” as if feeling and doing could be cleanly separated when you are the son sitting eleven thousand kilometres and one closed border away from the person you love.
I did not have a good answer.
Neither did he.

We had, instead, the beginning of a permanent, low-grade calculation that would run under every decision either of us made for the rest of our father’s life: how much can we actually do from here, how much is our mother carrying that we are not, how much of our absence is genuinely unavoidable and how much of it is a story we are telling ourselves so we don’t have to look directly at the unavoidable parts.

We agreed, that day, on the practical things — money, sent through a cousin, for a woman to come in the afternoons as well as the mornings; a doctor; a schedule of calls neither of us fully believed we could keep.
We did not discuss, because there is no efficient way to discuss it over a phone call already crowded with logistics, the actual shape of what was coming.
He fell again in November.
This time the hip went.

There was an operation, in a hospital in the north of the city that my mother went to every day for eleven days and described to me, at my request, in a detail that I have since wished I had not asked for — the corridor, the ward, the specific way my father lay in the bed with his good hand on top of the blanket as if he were holding it down.
He did not recover from it well.
Men of sixty-five with his sugar and his weight and his heart do not, as a rule, and the doctors said so, gently, in the register doctors use when the news is also the prognosis.

He came home in December to the house in Mirdamad and to a hospital bed that my mother had bought — I want that on the record, plainly: the woman he had divorced fourteen years earlier went to a medical supply shop on Vali Asr and bought her ex-husband the bed he was going to die in, and had it delivered, and had it put in his mother’s old room, because that was the room with the window — and he did not, from the day he was carried into that bed, get out of it again on his own feet.
My mother told me, weeks later, what the neurologist’s office had actually been like, since it was she who had taken him, in a wheelchair, in a taxi, before the second fall.

She described a small waiting room with the same generic posters you’d find anywhere in the world, and my father sitting very upright in the chair, dressed, she said, more formally than the appointment required, as if he’d decided that whatever was about to be said to him deserved a collar and pressed trousers.

When the doctor explained, gently, what the tests suggested — the word for it, the one you are thinking of, the one his own father had spent two years disappearing into while nobody in the family said it aloud — my father had listened without interrupting, genuinely rare for him, my mother pointed out, a man who interrupted waiters mid-sentence to correct their pronunciation of a dish, and had then asked exactly one question, which was not about prognosis or treatment or timeline, but “Will I still know my mother’s kitchen?” The doctor, my mother said, hadn’t had a ready answer for that one, and my father had nodded once, as if the lack of an answer was itself the answer, and asked when they could be done so he could go and find something to eat.
I called him myself the week of the appointment.

He was, that day, entirely himself — sharp, mildly annoyed about something at the pharmacy, uninterested in discussing his own diagnosis beyond a brief, dismissive wave of a sentence: “The doctors like to give things names.
It doesn’t change what I’m having for lunch.” And then, because he could not help himself, because the sarcasm was the last organ in him to fail: “Cheshmam roshan.
First the sugar, then the arm, now the head.
I’m collecting them.
Tell your brother I’ll have the full set by spring.” I let him have that.

The face with the flat hand is still there.

Seven in the morning in Los Angeles, half past six in the evening in Mirdamad.

What I’d eaten.
A mildly annoying conversation with a colleague.
The weather, in tedious, granular detail, the kind of detail no one requests and no one usually wants.

Yours.

I don’t think it’s the kind of thing that resolves.

I do not know whether my father found any peace in that forgetting.

I know only that from the outside, on a screen, in the last weeks, there had been a stillness in his face that looked, at certain angles, almost like the calm of someone who had finally put something down.

I thought of it, standing in front of the photograph, as a doorway rather than an ending — not because I believe, particularly, in doorways, but because it was the only image that let me hold both halves of it at once: the son who wanted to keep him, and the son who understood, eventually, that the kindest thing left to want, for a man who had run out of quality of life long before he ran out of life, was for the door to finally open.
I did not cry at this gathering, the way I had at the first one.

I stood for a while longer in front of the photograph, said nothing that anyone else could hear, and then went to find my brother, because there was, after everything, still a whole family left on this side of the door, on two continents, in two kitchens, and someone needed to ask what was for dinner.
EPILOGUE
[INTERIOR — SPECULATION]
Nobody can know what this was actually like from the inside, and this book has said so already, more than once.
What follows is offered in that same spirit — not as claimed fact, but as the only kind of understanding still available to the people left holding the question.
There must have been alert moments, even near the end.

Not many, and not for long, but the doctors said as much, gently, the way doctors learn to say things that are both a comfort and a warning at once: that recognition can flicker back briefly, unpredictably, like a signal catching a tower it had drifted out of range of.

In those moments, if they happened the way we hope they happened, I like to imagine it was something like surfacing — not confusion clearing all at once, but a single window opening in a house otherwise gone dark, just long enough to feel warmth arrive through it before it closed again.
A voice saying his name.
A flat hand on a blanket that felt like it belonged to someone.

Perhaps, for a few seconds, something almost like being him again — not enough to organise a sentence, not enough to reach for the phone himself and send the three hundredth message of the day, but enough, maybe, to feel loved without needing to understand exactly why, or by whom, or for how long that feeling might last before the window shut.

I hope, in those moments, that what reached him wasn’t the news itself — not the specific fact of a flat with light in it, or a room with a wall of names, or a fern on a sill — but the tone underneath the news, the register of a voice trying, across an impossible distance, to hand him something good.
I think tone might survive longer than meaning does.

I have to believe that, because it’s the only version of those one-sided phone calls I can live with: that some current of this is good, this is us, this is us wanting you here for it got through, even on the calls where nothing in his face moved at all.

And there must have been the other moments too — many more of them, by the end, than the alert ones — the ones the illness itself made, the long stretches where nothing organised enough to call a thought was happening at all.
I don’t think this was darkness, exactly, though it would be easy to assume so from outside a hospital bed.
Darkness requires a boundary, an edge you can sense yourself pressed against.
I think it might have been closer to what a candle experiences before being lit — not suffering, not absence exactly, just an interval with no experiencer present to suffer through it.
Time, if it existed for him at all in those stretches, might not have passed the way it passes for the rest of us, second stacked on second.

It might have simply not been happening, the way it isn’t happening for a stone, or for the year 1962, or for any of the countless hours of our own lives we’ve already forgotten completely without ever once mourning the loss of them.
That thought used to frighten me.
It doesn’t anymore, or not in the same way.

Because if that’s true — if those long stretches truly were closer to nothing than to suffering — then some of what looked, from our side of the phone, like the cruellest possible ending, may have been, from his side, no ending at all.
Just an absence with no one inside it left to be afraid of the dark.
A bed by a window.
Warm light through fabric.
A smell that might be saffron, or might only be the memory of a memory of it.

And then, simply, a door — unremarkable, unhurried, standing very slightly open, the way a door stands open in a house where someone is expected home any minute, the way a certain door in a certain apartment in Elahieh used to stand open, eight floors up, on the evenings a boy in a thin jacket was late.
He goes through it.
Nothing comes back to tell us, with certainty, which of these it was — the surfacing or the stone, the window or the interval with no one behind it.
Perhaps, at the very end, it was neither, and simply became, for the first time in years, entirely his own business again.
